title-group.article-title: Unveiling the effects of GSK126 on osteosarcoma cells implications for apoptosis, autophagy, and cellular migration

abstract.p: Osteosarcoma, a malignant bone tumor, faces significant treatment challenges. Enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2) shows aberrant expression in various tumors including osteosarcoma, which is identified as a potential therapeutic target. The anti-cancer efficacy of EZH2 inhibitor GSK126 has attracted attention, yet its impact on osteosarcoma cells was not fully understood. The study investigated the effects of GSK126 on osteosarcoma cells, particularly in apoptosis, autophagy, and cell motility. Our findings revealed that GSK126 induced apoptosis and autophagy, evidenced by increased markers like cleaved caspase-3 and LC3-II, and decreased cellular migration, through downregulation of the Fuse Binding Protein 1 (FBP1)/C-Myc axis. These findings suggest GSK126 as a promising therapeutic against osteosarcoma, offering a dual action of promoting cell death and hindering migration.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Osteosarcoma, primarily affecting adolescents and young adults, is a highly aggressive form of cancer marked by rapid proliferation and metastasis [1]. Its cause is complex and remains elusive [2]. Contemporary treatment modalities encompass a regimen of systemic chemotherapy coupled with extensive surgical resection [3]. Advancements in aggressive systemic chemotherapy regimens have bolstered survival rates, underscoring the exigency of novel therapeutic avenues for combating metastatic osteosarcoma [2].

The Enhancer of Zeste Homolog 2 (EZH2), integral to the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2), is pivotal in orchestrating gene expression through histone modification [4]. Overexpression of EZH2, observed across a myriad of cancers, is congruent with a more aggressive disease trajectory, dismal prognosis, and diminished survival rates [4]. EZH2 is a promising target for osteosarcoma treatment, leading to many potential inhibitors including GSK343 [5, 6], DZNeP [7], Tazemetostat [8], GSK126 [9]. GSK126, a potent and highly selective small-molecule inhibitor of EZH2 methyltransferase, diminishes trimethylation levels of lysine 27 on histone H3 (H3K27me3), an epigenetic hallmark typically conferred by EZH2 [10]. The molecular denomination of GSK126 is S)−1-(sec-butyl)-N-((4,6-diMethyl-2-oxo-1,2-dihydropyridin-3-yl) Methyl)−3-Methyl-6-(6-(piperazin-1-yl) pyridin-3-yl)−1H-indole-4-carboxaMide (C31H38N6O2, MW: 526.67, CAS: 1,346,574-57-9). Operating as a methionine-competitive histone lysine methyltransferase inhibitor, GS selectively and directly curtails the activity or expression of EZH2. Previous reports accentuated the potential of GS against a range of cancers including gastric cancer [11], diffuse large B-cell lymphoma [12], head and neck cancer [13], lung adenocarcinoma [14] and colorectal cancer [15]. In the current study, In order to increase our understanding on GSK126 as a molecule for clinical osteosarcoma treatment, we focus on GSK126 hypothesizing that it can significantly modulate osteosarcoma cellular, including cell apoptosis, autophagy and migration. In the present investigation, we endeavor to deepen our comprehension of GSK126 as a candidate molecule for clinical osteosarcoma management, postulating that it can significantly influence osteosarcoma cellular processes, encompassing cell apoptosis, autophagy, and migration.

sec.title: Reagents and cell culture
sec.p: GSK126 was obtained from Selleck Chemicals (Houston, TX, USA). Human osteosarcoma cell lines Saos-2 and U2OS were acquired from the Shanghai Cell Bank of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (Shanghai, China). Penicillin and streptomycin were sourced from Hyclone (Logan, Utah, USA). Saos-2 cells thrived in high-glucose DMEM medium from Gibco (Grand Island, NY, USA), supplemented with 10% FBS, 100 U/mL of both penicillin and streptomycin, incubated at 37 °C in a 5% CO2 atmosphere.

The apoptosis detection kits were obtained from KeyGen Biotech (Nanjing, Jiangsu, China). Total cellular protein extraction and BCA protein quantification kits were supplied by Beyotime Biotechnology (Shanghai, China), and ThermoFisher Scientific (Rockford, IL, USA), respectively. Antibodies targeting GAPDH, EZH2, p62, PARP, LC3, and cleaved caspase-3 were provided by Cell Signaling Technology (Danvers, MA, USA). Antibodies targeting FBP1 and C-Myc were obtained from Abcam (Cambridge, England, U.K.),

sec.title: Cell viability assay
sec.p: Saos2 and U2OS cells were inoculated at a density of 5.0 × 10^3 cells/well in a 96-well plate and incubated overnight. Subsequent to this, the cells were exposed to varying concentrations of GSK126, ranging from 0 to 15 μM, for a duration of 48 h. The cellular viability was ascertained via the MTS inner salt method, following the protocol of the Cell Titer 96 Aqueous One Solution Viability assay (Promega Corporation, Madison, WI, USA). This procedure was reiterated a minimum of three times.

sec.title: Flow cytometric assay
sec.p: The Annexin V-FITC/propidium iodide (PI) dual-staining protocol was employed to evaluate apoptosis in both Saos2 and U2OS cells. Post-inoculation in a 6-well plate, Saos2 cells were subjected to varying GSK126 concentrations for 48 h. Post-treatment, cells from each group were stained as per the kit's guidelines. Apoptotic cell counts were gauged via flow cytometry and subsequently analyzed with CellQuest™ software (Becton–Dickinson, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA). This experimental approach was conducted in triplicate.

sec.title: Western blot analysis
sec.p: Following a 48-h treatment with varied GSK126 concentrations, both Saos2 and U2OS cells were collected. The cells were lysed in an adapted RIPA buffer (comprising 150 mM NaCl, 1% NP-40, 50 mM Tris–Cl at pH 8.0, and 0.1% SDS), enhanced with protease, phosphatase inhibitor, and 1 mM PMSF from ThermoFisher Scientific. Following swift homogenization, the mixture was subjected to a 30-min ice incubation and then centrifuged at 12,000 g for 15 min at 4 °C. Protein concentrations were determined via BCA assay. Approximately 40 μg of protein per well was resolved on a 12% SDS-PAGE and electrotransferred to a PVDF membrane (Merck Millipore, Carrigtwohill, CO, USA). The membranes were subsequently blocked with 5% skim milk in TBST for an hour at ambient temperature, incubated with specific primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C, followed by a one-hour incubation with secondary antibodies at room temperature. ECL luminescence assay was employed for protein expression detection (Pierce, Rockford, IL, USA), and the relative protein abundance was quantified via densitometry using Quantity One 4.6.7 software (Bio-Rad, Philadelphia, PA, USA).

sec.title: Immunofluorescence assay
sec.p: Saos2 and U2OS cells, post their 48-h treatment with varying GSK126 concentrations, were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min, rinsed in PBS, blocked with 10% normal goat serum, and incubated with a 1:100 dilution of rabbit polyclonal antibody against human LC3 overnight at 4 °C. Dylight 594-conjugated anti-rabbit IgG was utilized at a 1:200 dilution for an hour at room temperature. Subsequent to counterstaining with DAPI for nuclei visualization, cells were promptly examined with a ZIESS confocal microscope (Oberkochen, Germany).

sec.title: Migration assay
sec.p: Saos2 and U2OS cells, upon reaching confluence in 6-well plates, were treated with 10 μg/ml mitomycin C (Sigma Aldrich; Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany) for two hours to inhibit cellular proliferation. A wound was then introduced into the cell monolayer using a pipette tip, followed by a PBS wash. DMEM, supplemented with 1% FBS, was added, and imagery was captured at the 48-h mark. Cellular migration distance was quantified as the wound width discrepancy between time zero and 48 h. This procedure was replicated in three independent trials.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All data were statistically examined using SPSS 17.0 software (SPSS, Chicago, IL, USA), with the results articulated as mean ± SD. The significance of discrepancies was computed via one-way ANOVA. A P-value less than 0.05 was deemed indicative of statistical significance.

sec.title: GSK126 impedes osteosarcoma cell proliferation
sec.p:
To evaluate the influence of GSK126 (Fig. 1A) on osteosarcoma cell proliferation, Saos2 and U2OS cells were exposed to a spectrum of GSK126 concentrations over 48 h. As illustrated in Fig. 1B, C, GSK126 potently curtailed osteosarcoma cell proliferation at concentrations of 5, 10, and 15 μM.Fig.1
GSK126 Restricts Osteosarcoma Cell Proliferation. A Depicts the chemical structure of GSK126. B, C Display the effects of varied GSK126 concentrations on Saos2 and U2OS cell proliferation over 48 h. *P < 0.05. **P < 0.01

sec.title: GSK126 provokes apoptosis in osteosarcoma cells
sec.p:
Utilizing annexin V-FITC/PI double-staining flow cytometry, we analyzed apoptosis (a manifestation of type I programmed cell death). Following a 48-h exposure to GSK126 (0, 5, 10, 15 μM), the apoptosis rates in Saos2 and U2OS cells exhibited a significant surge at 5–15 μM compared to the control group (0 μM), respectively (P < 0.05) (Fig. 2A–D).Fig. 2
GSK126 Promotes Apoptosis in Osteosarcoma Cells. A, B Visual representations of apoptosis in Saos2 and U2OS cells, respectively, using the Annexin V/PI assay, following a 48-h treatment with GSK126 at specified concentrations. C, D Quantitative data showing the rate of apoptosis in the treated Saos2 and U2OS cells. *P < 0.05. ***P < 0.001

Probing further, apoptotic markers—cleaved caspase-3 and ADP-ribose polymerase (PARP)—were discerned via western blot. A noticeable surge in the expressions of cleaved caspase-3 and PARP was observed with escalating GSK126 concentrations when juxtaposed with the control (Fig. 3A–F).Fig. 3
GSK126 Increases the Expression of Apoptosis Related Proteins PARP and C-Caspase3 in Osteosarcoma Cells. (A and D) Western blot assays displaying the levels of apoptosis-associated proteins (PARP and C-Caspase3) in Saos2 and U2OS cells treated with GSK126. (B and E) Quantitative data showing PARP expression levels in the treated Saos2 and U2OS cells. (C and F) Quantitative data showing C-Caspase3 expression levels in the treated Saos2 and U2OS cells. *P < 0.05. **P < 0.01. ***P < 0.001

sec.title: GSK126 triggers autophagy in osteosarcoma cells
sec.p:
Autophagy, a cellular mechanism for the lysosomal degradation of proteins and organelles, is implicated in type II programmed cell death, acting potentially as a tumor suppressive pathway. In our quest to discern if GSK126 instigates autophagy, we examined the GSK126-mediated activation and translocation of LC3-II to the autophagosome. Immunoblotting revealed augmented LC3-II accumulation in the autophagosomes of Saos2 and U2OS cells, correlating with GSK126 dosages, most conspicuously at 15 μM (Fig. 4A, B). Concurrently, p62, akin to LC3, serves as a hallmark for autophagic death detection. To gauge autophagy levels, we assessed the LC3-II/LC3-I ratio and p62 expression in Saos2 and U2OS cells post 48-h exposure to varied GSK126 concentrations. With incremental GSK126 levels, a discernible decline in p62 protein (Fig. 4C, D, F and G) was paralleled by a rise in LC3-II protein and LC3-II/I ratio (Fig. 4C, E, F and G). Both the attenuation of p62 and the LC3-II induction demonstrated GSK126 dose-responsiveness, with pronounced changes evident at a 5–15 μM concentration.Fig. 4
GSK126 Triggers Autophagy in Osteosarcoma Cells. (A, B) Immunofluorescence images showing LC3-II puncta formation in Saos2 and U2OS cells, respectively, after 48-h treatment with GSK126. The cells were co-stained with DAPI, highlighting the nuclei. Arrows pinpoint LC3-II puncta. (C and F) Western blot results indicating the expressions of autophagy-related proteins p62, LC3-I, and LC3-II in treated Saos2 and U2OS cells. (D and G) Quantitative data showing p62 expression levels in the treated Saos2 and U2OS cells. (E & H) Quantitative data showing LC3-II/I ratio in the treated Saos2 and U2OS cells. *P < 0.05. **P < 0.01. ***P < 0.001

sec.title: GSK126 attenuates osteosarcoma cell migration
sec.p:
Cellular migration is pivotal for cancerous invasion and metastasis. Through wound-healing assays, we examined the impact of GSK126 on osteosarcoma cell migration. Following GSK126 treatment, cell migrations across the void in monolayer cultures over a 48-h span were monitored. GSK126 conspicuously impeded the migration of Saos2 and U2OS cells, exhibiting a dose-responsive behavior (Fig. 5). Notably, the 5–15 μM GSK126-mediated migration inhibition was more profound compared to the control group (P < 0.001), underscoring the potential of GSK126 in mitigating osteosarcoma cell migration.Fig. 5
GSK126 Impedes Osteosarcoma Cell Migration. A, B Visuals from a wound healing assay over a 48-h period, contrasting the effects of different concentrations of GSK126 on cell migration. C, D The data quantification of the assay, showing the inhibitory effect of GSK126 on Saos2 and U2OS cell migration, as measured by the decrease in wound width over time. **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001

sec.title: GSK126 suppresses the FBP1/C-Myc axis in osteosarcoma cells
sec.p:
To clarify the underlying mechanism of GSK126 suppresses osteosarcoma development, we detected several regulators by western blot in Saos2 and U2OS cells (Fig. 6A and E). The expression level of EZH2 was inhibited by GSK126 in Saos-2 and U2OS cells in a dose-dependent manner, respectively (Fig. 6A, B, and Fig. 6E, F). The expression level of C-Myc, as a target protein of EZH2, was inhibited by GSK126 in Saos-2 and U2OS cells in a dose-dependent manner, respectively (Fig. 6A and D), and Fig. 6E and H). Because C-Myc is also a target protein of FBP1, the expression level of FBP1 was also detected, which was also suppressed by GSK126 in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. 6A and C), and Fig. 6E and G). These results suggested that GSK126 suppressed FBP1/C-Myc axis in osteosarcoma cells.Fig. 6
GSK126 Reduces the Expression of FBP1/C-Myc Axis in Osteosarcoma Cells. A and E Western blot assays displaying the levels of EZH2, FBP1 and C-Myc in Saos2 and U2OS cells treated with GSK126. B and F Quantitative data showing EZH2 expression levels in the treated Saos2 and U2OS cells. C and G Quantitative data showing FBP1 expression levels in the treated Saos2 and U2OS cells. D and H Quantitative data showing C-Myc expression levels in the treated Saos2 and U2OS cells. *P < 0.05. **P < 0.01. ***P < 0.001

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Cancer development and progression is a multifaceted process, not just governed by genetic mutations affecting oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, and DNA repair genes, but also significantly influenced by epigenetic changes [16–18]. EZH2 stands out in the epigenetic landscape due to its ability to modulate gene expression without altering the DNA sequence, primarily through its histone methyltransferase activity, which adds methyl groups to histone proteins, leading to chromatin remodeling and subsequent gene silencing [19, 20].

The discovery of EZH2 overexpression across various cancers has led to the development of targeted therapies [21, 22], with EZH2 inhibitors like GSK126 emerging as promising candidates. These inhibitors, particularly GSK126, function by directly competing with the substrate of EZH2, leading to reduced EZH2 activity and, thus, an anti-tumor effect by reactivating genes suppressed by EZH2-mediated methylation. Presently, limited investigations have delved into the potency of GSK126 against solid tumors, including but not limited to ovarian [23], Gastric cancer [14], and colorectal malignancies [9]. However, the efficacy of GSK126 is still under exploration in solid tumors.

Apoptosis, often referred to as type I programmed cell death, is a vital physiological process for maintaining tissue homeostasis, defending against disease, and sculpting the body during development [24, 25]. Dysfunction in apoptotic processes also contribute to the development of diseases [26]. Caspase-3 and PARP are two key indicators of apoptosis. Caspase-3 is a crucial executioner of apoptosis, and its cleaved form signifies active apoptosis. PARP, on the other hand, is involved in DNA repair, and its cleaved form is another hallmark of ongoing apoptosis [27, 28]. Our investigation revealed that GSK126 triggers apoptosis in Saos2 and U2OS cells in a dose-responsive paradigm. Specifically, concentrations of 10 and 15 μM of GSK126 markedly escalated apoptosis in both cell lines. Concurrently, there was an appreciable upsurge in the biomarkers presiding over apoptosis, embodied by cleaved caspase-3 and PARP.

Autophagy, a crucial cellular self-digestion process, aids cells in sustaining homeostasis by systematically degrading and recycling cytoplasmic debris and dysfunctional components [29, 30]. This mechanism, fundamental for cellular adaptation to stress, toggles between being a survival mechanism under certain thresholds and a form of programmed cell death—termed type II—when excessively activated [31]. Central to the autophagy pathway are biomolecules like LC3 and p62. LC3 exists in two forms: LC3-I and LC3-II. During autophagy, LC3-I conjugates with phosphatidylethanolamine to form LC3-II, migrating to the autophagosome membranes, a step crucial for autophagosome formation [29]. Thus, the presence and increase of LC3-II serve as a marker for autophagic activity. Conversely, p62—a cargo receptor for autophagic degradation—diminishes during autophagy, making its decreasing levels another indicator of ongoing autophagy [29]. The study reveals a dose-dependent increase in LC3-II alongside a decrease in p62 levels upon GSK126 treatment, hinting at the drug's role in intensifying autophagic activity. This is further corroborated by immunofluorescence, which illustrate an uptick in autophagosome numbers—a hallmark of autophagic cell death—in response to escalating GSK126 concentrations. By shedding light on the capacity of GSK126 to induce autophagic cell death, these observations underscore the drug's potential therapeutic angle, particularly in cancer treatment strategies where manipulating autophagic pathways could be pivotal.

Indeed, cellular migration is a critical factor in the progression of cancer, particularly in the processes of invasion and metastasis. The reduction in cell migration suggests potential anti-metastatic properties [32, 33]. In the current study, GSK126 effectively reduces osteosarcoma cell migration in a concentration-dependent manner, it might be considered as part of a therapeutic strategy for patients with advanced or metastatic osteosarcoma, especially those who are not responding to standard therapies.

Research has revealed a complex interplay between EZH2 and C-Myc, underscoring the multifaceted role of C-Myc as a pivotal oncogene integral to cellular processes such as growth regulation, differentiation, and apoptosis. There is a positive correlation between the expression of EZH2 and C-Myc in the breast cancer [34, 35], and we have previously found a physical binding relationship between them [5, 6]. Notably, aberrant expression of C-Myc is implicated in a myriad of tumors [36]. C-Myc functions as a transcription factor that modulates gene expression, utilizing various mechanisms such as recruiting histone acetyltransferases, chromatin remodeling proteins and DNA methyltransferases [37]. Furthermore, the regulation of C-Myc expression is activated by FBP1 through its interaction with the far-upstream element (FUSE) element of the C-Myc operator. Our previous research results indicated that a mutual regulatory mechanism between FBP1 and EZH2 expression, that is to say that EZH2 knockdown significantly inhibited FBP1 expression, and FBP1 knockdown also decreased the expression of EZH2 [6]. In addition, FBP1 increases proliferation and cisplatin resistance of ovarian cancer cells through up-regulating EZH2-mediated H3K27me3 [4]. This study demonstrates that GSK126 effectively diminishes the levels of EZH2, C-Myc, and FBP1 in a dose-responsive manner. Consequently, GSK126's therapeutic potential against osteosarcoma is partially attributed to its suppression of the FBP1/C-Myc signaling pathway. The principal findings are encapsulated in Fig. 7.Fig. 7
Mechanism Hypothesis: GSK126 Promotes Apoptosis and Autophagy of Osteosarcoma Cells and Inhibits Cell Migration by Inhibiting the FBP1/C-Myc Axis

While this study provides valuable insights into the role of GSK126 and its impact on the FBP1/C-Myc axis, a significant limitation is the lack of in vivo experiments in animal models to validate these findings. The results obtained from in vitro studies, although compelling, may not fully recapitulate the complex interactions present in a living organism, including the tumor microenvironment, systemic effects, and pharmacokinetics of the drug. Future research should prioritize in vivo studies to confirm the efficacy and safety of GSK126 in relevant animal models. Such experiments would allow for a more comprehensive understanding of how GSK126 affects tumor growth, metastasis, and response to therapy in a dynamic biological context. Furthermore, in vivo validation could provide insights into potential side effects and help refine dosing strategies, ultimately enhancing the translational potential of this research.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Our results showed that pharmacologic inhibition of EZH2 by GSK126 not only significantly induced apoptosis and autophagic cell death in osteosarcoma cells, but also reduced the migration of osteosarcoma cells. Mechanistically, GSK126 is at least partly mediated through its inhibitory activity on the FBP1/C-Myc signaling axis. These findings provide an important biological basis for further research on the application of GSK126 in the treatment of osteosarcoma.
